# The ggplot2 phrasebook

ggplot2 proved that a grammar of graphics could be a working tool and not only a
theory. Most readers of this book already know it. gog follows the same grammar
and decides the details differently. This appendix answers two questions: what to
write in gog, and what behaves differently. The ggplot2 calls on this page
are those of ggplot2 4.0.3 [@wickham2026ggplot2pkg].

The translations assume gog can draw the plot you want. To find out whether it
can, read [Coverage](coverage.qmd). That appendix compares ggplot2's whole
reference index with gog's [kernel](grammar.qmd#the-kernel), in both
directions: what gog draws that ggplot2 does not, and what ggplot2 draws that
gog does not.

## Side by side

This first table compares the two systems as a whole, rather than term by term.

| | ggplot2 | gog |
|---|---|---|
| Languages | R | R, Python, Julia and JavaScript, all four calling one engine |
| Naming | `geom_point`, `aes`, `alpha` | `point`, channels by plain name, `opacity` |
| Where `x`/`y` are written | `aes()` at the plot or the layer, and a layer may override the plot's `aes()` | before any mark, for every layer; after a mark, for that mark. A layer with no column of its own reads the first column written for that axis. |
| The histogram | `geom_histogram()` *or* `stat_bin(geom = "bar")` | `bar * bin` |
| Log axis | `scale_x_log10()` | `x(gdp, scale = "log")`, written on the binding |
| 3-D | external packages | one more position: `z` |
| Animation | gganimate, a separate package | `play` is a channel of the kernel: `+ play(year)` |

## Translations

This table is term by term. Find the ggplot2 call on the left; the gog spelling
that does the same job is beside it on the right.

| You write in ggplot2 | You write in gog |
|---|---|
| `ggplot(df, aes(x = a, y = b))` | `data(df) + x(a) + y(b) + …` |
| `geom_point()` | `point` |
| `geom_line()` | `line` |
| `geom_step()` | `step` |
| `geom_area()` | `area` |
| `geom_col()` | `bar`, one bar per row; with several rows per category, `bar * sum` gives their total |
| `geom_bar()`, which counts the rows for you | `bar * count`, because `bar` alone counts nothing |
| `geom_histogram(bins = 30)` | `bar * bin(30)` |
| `geom_freqpoly()` | `line * bin` |
| `geom_density()` | `line * density` |
| `geom_smooth()` | `ribbon * smooth_band + line * smooth`: the band and the curve are two layers. `smooth` fits a straight line locally and `geom_smooth()` fits a parabola, so the two curves can differ where the relationship is curved ([LOESS trend line](transforms.qmd#smooth-loess-trend-line)) |
| `geom_smooth(se = FALSE)` | `line * smooth`: the curve of the row above, without its band |
| `stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "bar")` | `bar * mean` |
| `geom_boxplot()` | `box`, which computes its own summary, as `geom_boxplot()` does |
| `geom_violin()` | `ribbon * density`, with the categories on `x`. The default shapes differ. gog's violins run past the data and narrow to a point, weight each area by row count, and share one bandwidth. `geom_violin()` cuts each end flat, draws equal areas, and gives each violin its own bandwidth. `density(compare = "shape")` gives equal areas ([Compared with ggplot2's violin](marks/ribbon.qmd#compared-with-ggplot2s-violin)) |
| `geom_jitter()` | `point * jitter`, on a categorical axis. On two continuous axes gog refuses it and suggests `style(opacity = )` instead. |
| `geom_errorbar()`, `geom_linerange()` | `interval * bounds(lower, upper)` for ends you already have, or `interval * confidence` to compute them; `style(caps = FALSE)` removes the caps, which gives a linerange |
| `geom_ribbon()` | `ribbon * bounds(lower, upper)` |
| `geom_tile()` | `zone + x(a) + y(b) + color(v)`, with `a` and `b` categorical: each category gets its own slot |
| `geom_hline()`, `geom_vline()` | `data(t) + rule + y(v)` for horizontal lines, and `x(v)` for vertical ones, where the table `t` holds the positions |
| `geom_text()` | `text + label(g)` |
| `geom_path()` | `path`, which joins the rows in the table's order |
| `aes(color = g)` | `color(g)` |
| `aes(fill = g)` | `color(g)`: one channel colors a bar's fill and a line's stroke, and there is no `fill` |
| `aes(size = v)` | `size(v)` |
| `aes(shape = g)` | `shape(g)` |
| `aes(alpha = v)` | `opacity(v)` |
| `aes(linetype = g)` | `pattern(g)`: a dash on a line, a hatch on a filled region |
| `aes(group = g)` | `group(g)` |
| `scale_x_log10()` | `x(v, scale = "log")` |
| `scale_color_viridis_c()` | `color(v) + palette("viridis")` |
| `scale_color_manual(values = c(a = "red", b = "blue"))` | `color(g) + palette(c(a = "red", b = "blue"))`: each color is written beside its category's name, so sorting the rows cannot change it. gog refuses a name the column does not hold and a category left without a name ([Colors by name](channels.qmd#colors-by-name)) |
| `guides(color = "none")`, `show.legend = FALSE` | `color(g, legend = FALSE)`, written on the channel whose legend you leave out |
| `facet_grid(r ~ c)` | `\| facet(c) / facet(r)` |
| `facet_wrap(~ g, ncol = 4)` | `\| facet(g, wrap = 4)` puts four panels in each row, and `/ facet(g, wrap = 4)` puts four in each column. The operator says the direction, so one number replaces both `nrow` and `ncol`. |
| `facet_*(scales = "free_y")` | `y(v, free = TRUE)`, written on the axis you are freeing. You do not choose the axis a second time, because the binding already says which one. |
| patchwork's <code>p1 &#124; p2</code>, `p1 / p2` | <code>plot_a &#124; plot_b</code>, `plot_a / plot_b`: the same two operators. What is written on the right decides what happens: a plot is placed beside or below, and a `facet()` splits the plot into panels. |
| ggrepel's `geom_text_repel()` | `text * repel`, one of the four collision modifiers, with `dodge`, `stack` and `jitter` |
| ggExtra's `ggMarginal()` | <code>top / (main &#124; right)</code>, three ordinary plots ([Composition](composition.qmd)) |
| patchwork's `plot_spacer()`, `plot_layout(widths = )` | `theme(width = )` on a plot placed beside others, or `theme(height = )` on one stacked above or below, in pixels; the plots that ask for nothing share what is left. In the marginal layout above, the empty corner needs no spacer. |
| `coord_flip()` | swap the `x` and `y` bindings: orientation is taken from whichever axis carries the categories, so there is nothing to switch |
| `coord_polar()` | `polar()` |
| `labs(title = , x = , y = )` | `title()`, `x_label()`, `y_label()`, `z_label()` |
| `color = "red"`, `alpha = 0.5` inside a `geom_*()` | `style(color = "red", opacity = 0.5)` |
| `theme(…)` | `theme()`, for what belongs to the whole plot rather than one layer, such as its size, gridlines and background; `style()` belongs to one layer |
| `ggsave("plot.svg")` | `save_svg(p, "plot.svg")`. gog draws every plot as SVG, so the file name must end in `.svg`. [Functions around the grammar](utilities.qmd#save_svg) shows the call, which is the same in every language. |

## Six differences to expect

The words translate, but six things work differently in gog.

- **`+` is still `+`, and on purpose.** ggplot2's author has said the pipe would
  have been the better interface [@wickham2018pipe]. gog chose `+` for two
  reasons. A pipe cannot be given a gog meaning: Python has no pipe operator,
  and the pipes of R and Julia already mean something else. A pipe also makes
  every atom a function, and `bar * bin` has no meaning once both sides are
  functions. [Operators](operators.qmd) covers this in full, including which
  atoms give the same plot in any order.
- **A count is a word you write.** `bar` draws your numbers unchanged.
  `geom_bar()` counts rows on its own, and gog counts only when you write a
  counting transform, such as `count` or `bin`. The one mark that computes by itself is `box`, because a box
  plot *is* a summary.
- **There is one spelling.** There are no geom/stat pairs, so you never choose
  between two functions. If two different atoms in gog do the same job, that
  is a bug: [report it](https://github.com/psychometrician/gog/issues) on the
  project's repository.
- **The scale belongs to the binding.** Options such as `scale`, `limits`,
  `free` and `legend` are arguments of the binding, as in
  `x(gdp, scale = "log")` or `color(g, legend = FALSE)`, and there is no
  `scale_*()` function. The colors of a color scale come from `palette()`, which
  belongs to the whole plot.
- **Setting is not mapping.** A constant maps no column, so it gets no legend.
  Write it in `style()`. In ggplot2 `aes(color = "red")` is legal and draws a
  legend with one entry called "red". Here a channel takes a column, not a
  value, so gog refuses `color("red")` and names `style(color = "red")` as the
  fix.
- **Refusals name the fix.** A sentence gog cannot draw is refused, and the
  message says what to change. Where ggplot2 warns about an unknown
  argument and draws anyway, gog stops and draws nothing. This book shows refusals on purpose: it
  runs the refused sentence and prints the message you would see.

If a call you use is in neither table, [Coverage](coverage.qmd) says whether
gog draws that plot at all.
